results.content: Additionally, we also investigate the effect of increasing noise levels and data length on the network measures and their distributions (in the case of vertex-based measures) for *ε*-recurrence networks derived from chaotic dynamics. Transitivity dimension (*a*), average path length (*b*) and assortativity (*c*) of the *ε*-recurrence networks constructed from the *x*-component of hyper-chaotic Rössler system (dashed blue lines) and corresponding iAAFT surrogates (solid red lines) for embedding dimension *m*=2and increasing data length *N* at recurrence rate RR=0.02. Transitivity dimension (*a*), average path length (*b*) and assortativity (*c*) of the *ε*-recurrence networks constructed from the *x*-component of hyper-chaotic Rössler system (dashed blue lines) and corresponding iAAFT surrogates (solid red lines) for embedding dimension *m*=2and increasing data length *N* at recurrence rate RR=0.02. The *ε*-recurrence networks constructed from chaotic systems contain more vertices that display high values of *b**i* (>3000 vertices with approximately 104 shortest paths) and (>3000 vertices with ⁠) compared with the *ε*-recurrence networks constructed from the stochastic dynamics in the case of the Lorenz attractor and the corresponding iAAFT surrogate (electronic supplementary material, figure S12). Looking at the distributions of *b**i* and for the hyper-chaotic Rössler attractor and the corresponding surrogate at *N*=10 000 and 20 000 (electronic supplementary material, figures S14 and S16), it is clear that the nodes acquiring high values of *b**i* and in *ε*-recurrence networks constructed from the hyper-chaotic Rössler system increases compared with the networks constructed from the corresponding iAAFT surrogates as data length is increased. Also, looking at the distributions of *c**i* and *k**i* (electronic supplementary material, figures S15 and S17 for *N*=10 000 and 20 000, respectively), we again observe that vertices of the *ε*-recurrence networks representing hyper-chaotic dynamics tend to acquire lower values of *c**i* compared with their stochastic counterparts for the same reason as outlined above for the chaotic case. Influence of noise levels on the clustering property of the *ε*-recurrence networks and the presence of unstable periodic orbits was evident with the increase in transitivity dimension ⁠, decrease in number of vertices with high values for local clustering coefficient and betweenness centrality *b**i* and disappearance of peaks (which is related to the UPOs) in the distribution of degree centrality *k**i*.

For true positives and false negatives, the adjusted strategy performed better than the unadjusted. For true negatives and false positives, the unadjusted strategy performed better. As one can see based on the true positives, the adjusted strategy has a higher average return than both the unadjusted and original strategies. When we run t-tests on the difference in means between the adjusted, unadjusted, and original strategies, we note that it is indeed the true positives and false negatives that show a significant difference between the adjusted and competing strategies based on p-values below the 0.05 threshold.

results.content: # False Positives and False Negatives in Drug Testing: Complete Guide. ovusmedical.com False Positives and False Negatives. # **False Positives & Negatives on a Drug Test Guide**. **False positives and false negatives in drug testing** are important to understand because drug tests, while powerful tools for workplace safety, healthcare, and personal use, are not always perfect. Certain medications, supplements, and even foods can interfere with results, leading to a false positive (a drug is detected when none was used) or a false negative (a drug is missed even though it was used). # **Can Medications or Foods Cause False Drug Test Results?**. Certain **medications, supplements, and even foods** can sometimes cause a **false positive**, while others can lead to a **false negative**—making it seem like a drug isn’t present when it actually is. A **false positive** happens when a test shows a positive result for a drug that the individual hasn’t used. ## **False Positives and False Negatives in Drug Testing by Drug**.

results.title: How to better control for false positives while monitoring your experiment
results.content:
Title: How to better control for false positives while monitoring your experiment
# How to better control for false positives while monitoring your experiment | by Anfisa Rovinsky | Data Science + AI at Microsoft | Medium. In this article I discuss how I developed two data sets to evaluate methods addressing peeking and multiple comparison testing to reduce false positives during the monitoring phase of an experiment. The second set simulated A/A tests to also generate scorecard history and provide true labeled data, though limited to true negatives and false positives. This approach is slightly more complex to implement, and though it has greater power than FWER, this mitigation comes at the cost of increased false negatives (lower power, ability to detect true positives). Although we have a history of experiments, we don’t truly have per-metric, per-scorecard labeled data identifying whether each one was a true positive, false positive, true negative, or false negative. The value in running an A/A test is that because we know there are no true differences between Treatment and Control, we can accurately evaluate the false positive rate given various mitigation techniques. An A/A scorecard can have only false positives (anything identified as statistically significant) and true negatives. *   Looking between the combination OBF and combination KDM approaches, we see overall that the combination OBF ones perform better than the combination KDM ones in terms of Precision, Recall and A/A False Positive Rate. *   Looking across the three B approaches (Bonferroni (B), Benjamini-Hochberg (BH), and Benjamini-Yekutieli (BY)) we likely have no real difference in terms of Precision and AA False Positive Rate, but it does look like BH has better Recall than both BY and B. Having developed two data sets we were able to reasonably evaluate the 11 approaches and identified Benjamini-Hochberg as the best mix in terms of performance, implementation cost, and maintenance. Today we use the Benjamini-Hochberg correction in creating an adjusted alpha for evaluating the relevant quality and health measure movements during the monitoring phase and have greatly reduced spurious false positives. The second set simulated A/A tests to also generate scorecard history and provide true labeled data, though limited to true positives and false positives.
